#4803. When the World Doesn't Say Thank You

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 8, 2026 | Reviewed by Jessica Schrader

For a while, one of the most reliable relationships in my life was with a traffic sign.

It was one of those electronic billboards you see on the outskirts of villages that nags you for how fast you're driving. Go too fast and the numbers flash red. Keep to the speed limit and you're rewarded with two words of appreciation:

I became a bit too fond of that sign. Embarrassingly, some days I would deliberately crawl past it, making sure I was going at exactly the right speed, just to receive its validation. And it delivered. Every time.

“You're most welcome,” I'd think, feeling absurdly pleased with myself.

Now, you might reasonably wonder why a mature woman would get quite so much satisfaction from being thanked by an illuminated slab of roadside equipment.

I'd recently returned from Switzerland, and was trying to find my feet in a community where I'd once felt very much at home. Much had changed in my absence, and cultivating a sense of belonging was proving difficult.

I was living alone, feeling bereft, and some days the only living creature I spoke to was an elderly cat. Not to be too judgy, but although he was selectively affectionate, his vocabulary wasn’t up to much. So the traffic sign became an accidental but welcome addition to my social circle.

I knew perfectly well that it was only thanking me for driving at the appropriate speed, but I looked forward to those two little words dropping into my day. It felt good to be acknowledged and, truthfully, I wanted some reassurance that I hadn't disappeared.

I've been reflecting on that period recently, and about how much we rely on other people to remind us who we are. It's a backdrop we barely notice when life is flowing along reasonably well. We have our familiar routines, people to talk to, and places to go. There's a sense of belonging that we probably take for granted until our circumstances change.

I think this is one of the reasons loneliness can be so unsettling. Alongside the sadness of having nobody to share things with, there's the strange experience of chalking up an entire day without anyone witnessing it.

You might have achieved something substantial, or white-knuckled your way through a thoroughly miserable morning. Maybe you made a particularly earthy soup with the leeks from your garden, and nobody noticed.

One unremarkable Tuesday, I remember calculating how long it would take my neighbors to realise I hadn’t collected the milk from my doorstep. Three days, I wagered.

Having written a book called Change Your Words, Change Your World, I've spent much of my working life exploring how language affects the way we feel about ourselves, so I’m quite familiar with the idea of self-worth. In theory, at least. In practice, knowing something intellectually doesn't necessarily mean you're proficient at applying it when life gets difficult.

Like you, no doubt, I've caught myself looking for digital reassurance. A message from someone I care about can lift my spirits enormously. Equally, the absence of a reply can fill my head with squirrels and I’ll waste a couple of hours wondering what I've done wrong.

Wanting to feel appreciated is human. The trouble is that other people are unreliable sources of reassurance because they have their own lives to get on with. Sometimes they’re just busy running a taxi service for their kids and don’t get your message until bedtime. Other times they’re having enthralling conversations with their own cats.

Meanwhile, we're wondering whether we've somehow offended the entire human race. It's exhausting. And I wonder how much of that exhaustion comes from constantly looking outside ourselves for something we might be able to offer ourselves.

We’re often much kinder to other people. If a friend tells us she's had a dreadful day, we don't usually ask her to produce evidence; we listen, sympathise, maybe make her a cup of tea. However, when it comes to our own shortcomings, we can be surprisingly dismissive.

Psychologist Kristin Neff has spent years researching self-compassion, including how we can learn to respond to our own challenges with the understanding we'd offer a friend.

It sounds perfectly sensible, doesn't it? But when you’re feeling lonely or discouraged, do you comfort yourself, or spend time forensically investigating what you’ve done to end up that way?

This year I’ve decided to take a different approach. Whenever that familiar feeling of being disappointed or overlooked colors my perspective, I pause and acknowledge what's actually happening.

Is it possible I was hoping someone would call, or do I just need a hug? There's often a little relief in admitting that, even if nothing changes immediately.

It doesn't always work, of course. Some days I'd like the universe to send me a personalised letter of appreciation, preferably on headed paper.

I wonder what I’d say now to the woman who used to drive past that traffic sign. I'd tell her I understood why she was lonely, and that it was perfectly reasonable to miss the life she'd had, even though she might not believe me.

Perhaps that's the thing about learning to validate ourselves. It's easy enough to understand the idea, but quite another matter to feel it. I don't think I've entirely worked it out yet, but I’m getting better at noticing when I’m waiting for someone else to tell me I’m doing all right.

It still feels a little unnatural, but then so did developing an emotional attachment to a traffic sign. I still smile whenever I drive past one and receive my THANK YOU. And I always make sure I'm going at the right speed. It would be a shame to disappoint an old friend.

Neff, K. D. (2003). Self-compassion: An alternative conceptualization of a healthy attitude toward oneself. Self and Identity, 2(2), 85–101. https://doi.org/10.1080/15298860390129863

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Pope Leo XIV has been diagnosed with lung cancer following a successful surgery, the Vatican said.

The Pope, 71, underwent surgery at Agostino Gemelli University Policlinic in Rome on October 13 to remove a nodule from his right lung. This was determined to be pulmonary adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer.

The surgeons removed the lower lobe of the Pope’s lung to “ensure a radical procedure; the lower lobe of the right lung was removed using a video-assisted technique,” said Dr. Luigi Carbone, the Director of Vatican Healthcare Services, and Professor Stephano Margaritora, the lead surgeon, in a press release.

“An intraoperative histological examination confirmed the diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma, as suspected from the preoperative examinations,” they said.

Pope Leo was in the operating room for 3 hours, while the operation itself lasted around 90 minutes.

The doctors noted that it was a successful operation with no complications.

According to Matteo Bruni, the Director of the Holy See Press Office, the Pope asked for dinner after the surgery and spent the evening with his secretaries and other Vatican staff.

In a press release on Wednesday, the Vatican said that the Pope’s postoperative recovery is progressing well.

According to Vatican News, Pope Leo had a calm first night following his surgery.

In the coming days, exams will be conducted on the removed tissue. There has currently been no change in the initially announced week of hospitalization.

On October 14, the Pope underwent blood tests and chest X-rays that were scheduled following his surgery. The results of these tests confirm that his postoperative recovery is progressing as expected, and the values are within a normal range for the type of operation performed.

Pope Leo has also undergone some respiratory physiotherapy and has begun walking around his room, the Vatican said.

It has not yet been announced whether he will require any further treatment.

Adenocarcinoma is the most common subtype of lung cancer globally. It accounts for around 40% of all lung cancer diagnoses.

Adenocarcinoma is a type of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), which accounts for about 80–85% of all lung cancers.

Lung adenocarcinoma begins in the epithelial cells that produce mucus. It is the most common type of NSCLC.

Adenocarcinoma can be classified further by the genetic changes driving the tumor. For example, EGFR-positive lung cancer is found more often in people who have never smoked and can often be treated with targeted therapies, which is why biomarker testing of tumor tissue helps guide treatment decisions.

Treatment for NSCLC is generally determined by the stage. However, it typically involves one or a combination of:

Surgery is generally the first step in treatment for this type of lung cancer. The right lung has three lobes, or sections, and the left has two.

A doctor will often remove the entire lobe that has the tumor in order to remove the tumor and improve the outlook.

The body eventually adapts in order to compensate for the loss of function.

According to the American Cancer Society (ACS), for NSCLC that hasn’t spread outside of the lung, the 5-year relative survival rate is 67%.

#4801. Are You Waiting for Life to Begin?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 8, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma

What if the person who brings you to life is also the one who brings you pain?

I was thinking about my own life and how, sometimes, it can feel as though it is divided into two halves: the life we live and the life we imagine sharing with a particular person.

When I tried to picture it, I saw a page divided by a crooked line (like the line in a broken-heart emoji). Another line runs alongside it, following its shape, inseparable from it. It was the connection, even when the two people were no longer together.

If you look at this picture, you might see different things. But I see three beings. Two who could not be more different, yet somehow belong to each other. And a third one: The space between them. The grey that separates their worlds, yet also connects them. That line is a boundary and a bridge.

Sometimes, light passes through that grey and reaches the other side, turning it bright for a moment. Life becomes colorful again. There is love, warmth, and a feeling that the world might be beautiful. But when the light fades, they return to their separate worlds, to the lives they have to live apart.

Maybe it is that space between the two moments, the third part of the picture, where you find yourself suspended in midair, unable to move forward or backward, not knowing where you stand.

One becomes the freedom. The other becomes the weight that gives that freedom meaning. But perhaps neither is as free as they seem. One does not know how to stop giving. The other does not know how to stop holding on. That is why some connections are so difficult to explain: they bring out parts of us we rarely see, beautiful, yet painful.

But what if the grey world in this picture is not only about the space between two people? What if it is also about the way we live?

Think about how much of our lives we spend waiting. Waiting for the right person, the right opportunity, the right moment. We look at our present lives and see only the grey. We imagine that once someone arrives, once we finally get what we have been longing for, we will begin to live.

But while we wait for that moment, what happens to the life we are already living?

We begin to believe that life is waiting for us somewhere in the future, beyond that line. This is why some connections are so powerful. For a moment, they remind us that we can feel something we thought we had lost. Something so human that, for a second, the rest of the world vanishes. We think we miss the person, but we miss the version of ourselves who felt that alive in their presence.

Have you ever considered that the person who awakened something inside you might not be the only place where that part of you can exist? What if the freedom, the love were yours all along, even before you met them? Maybe they helped you discover a part of yourself you never knew existed.

The connection was real. What you felt was real. It could have been painful, beautiful, and unlike anything you had experienced before. None of that becomes less meaningful just because the connection ended. But why do we have to hold on to the person to keep what they helped us discover?

Maybe it is possible to let someone go without having to erase what happened. Keep the part of yourself that came alive. You do not have to return to the connection to feel those things again. You can carry them into the rest of your life.

I know that looking inside yourself isn't comfortable. It means accepting some things, questioning others, and making sense of your own feelings. It also means recognizing that a new person is not responsible for the pain left by someone who came before them.

I would tell my younger self that it is okay not to have everything figured out. It is okay to take your time. And it is okay to miss someone without going back to them.

And if you are living in the grey right now, remember that the part of you that can see the light is still there. You may have stopped looking for it. Sometimes, all you need is to believe that the other side exists. But life on the grey side can be beautiful, too, if you allow yourself to see it. An ordinary morning can be warmth, joy in a small moment, and beauty in places you might have overlooked. And when you finally see it, let yourself feel it fully.

You might ask, what is the point of all this? Well, first of all, thank you for reading almost to the end. But if I had to leave you with just one thought, it's this: no matter where you are, whom you are with, or what circumstances you are living through, your life is still yours. You may not always have a choice about what happens, but you have some choice in how you meet it. You can spend your days holding on to what hurts, waiting for life to be different, or you can slowly begin noticing the beautiful things that are already here.

There is life everywhere, even in the dirt. And no, that doesn't mean we have to pretend everything is fine or feel grateful for every difficult thing that happens. It means that even in an imperfect life, there is still something worth noticing.

Your light is always there, with you. You do not have to spend your life waiting for someone else to turn it on.

#4800. This 61-Year-Old Is in the Shape of His Life—and Credits This Exercise with Transforming His Chest

Ricky Dietrich says the incline cable pullover has been a game changer.

A stronger chest isn't built through endless bench pressing and cable flys alone. Sometimes, adding a less obvious movement to your routine can provide a completely different stimulus.

At 61, Ricky Dietrich claims he's in the best shape of his life, and one exercise he credits with helping build his chest is the incline cable pullover.

“This is one of the only exercises I owe my lower chest growth to,” he says. “It keeps constant tension through the entire rep, lets me push close to failure safely, and has been one of the biggest contributors to building a fuller lower chest.”

While Dietrich describes it as a lower-chest exercise, pullovers aren't quite that simple. Depending on your setup and technique, both your chest and lats can contribute to the movement, with small adjustments changing where you feel the exercise most.

The incline cable pullover is a variation of the classic dumbbell pullover, a movement famously championed by Arnold Schwarzenegger and his Golden Era contemporaries.

Dietrich's version swaps the dumbbell for a cable machine and performs the movement on an incline bench. The cable keeps tension on the working muscles throughout more of the range of motion, rather than allowing the resistance to drop away at certain points.

Technique matters, particularly if you want to bias the chest rather than allowing your lats to dominate.

Dietrich recommends beginning with your arms overhead, keeping them relatively close together and maintaining a proud chest as you pull the cable forwards. Rather than continuing until your hands reach your hips, stop while your arms are still roughly 45 degrees from your torso, squeezing your pecs hard.

Allowing your elbows to flare and driving them further towards your sides can shift more of the work towards your lats. Using a lighter load should also make it easier to control the movement and concentrate on the muscles you're trying to target.

Think of the incline cable pullover as an accessory rather than a replacement for your presses and flys. But if your chest training has become stale, it could provide a useful new angle.

#4799. Ultra-Processed Food Intake May Not Be Linked to Colorectal Cancer

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Ultra-processed foods as a group do not increase the risk of colorectal cancer, according to a new study.

Researchers from the National Cancer Institute (NCI) report that they found no association between overall intake of ultra-processed foods and colorectal cancer incidence among the more than 400,000 adults they studied.

They said their findings are important because ultra-processed foods now account for more than half of adults’ energy intake in the United States. They published their research on October 15 in PLOS Medicine.

The study comes amid recent research that has connected ultra-processed foods to an increased risk of heart disease, type 2 diabetes, and obesity.

However, the link between colorectal cancer and ultra-processed foods has been less clear.

A 2025 study reported that ultra-processed foods may increase the risk of colorectal cancer in females under 50.

A 2022 study found that males who consumed high rates of ultra-processed foods had a higher risk of developing colorectal cancer.

NCI scientists noted in their new study that ultra-processed products represent a wide range of foods.

They pointed out that foods such as whole grains and dairy products were associated with a lower risk of colorectal cancer among study participants, while foods such as processed meats were associated with a higher risk.

“We did not observe an association between total ultra-processed food (UPF) intake and colorectal cancer incidence,” said Erikka Loftfield, PhD, a former investigator with the NCI, in a news release. “However, when we looked at food groups, like whole grains, dairy, and meat, by UPF or non-UPF source, we found that associations were in line with current dietary guidance for colorectal cancer prevention.”

Experts not involved in the study told Healthline that the NCI scientists appear to be on the right track.

“While the study did not find that overall ultra-processed food intake was associated with colorectal cancer risk, the findings suggest that simply classifying foods by their level of processing may not tell the whole story,” said Marissa Shams-White, PhD, a senior principal scientist in population science at the American Cancer Society.

“One of the challenges with studying ultra-processed foods is that the category includes a very wide range of foods and beverages, and we don’t yet know whether they all relate to colorectal cancer risk in the same way,” she added.

Ketan Thanki, MD, a colorectal surgeon specializing in benign and malignant diseases of the colon, rectum, and anus at the MemorialCare Todd Cancer Institute at Long Beach Medical Center in California, agrees.

“Just because it is ultra-processed doesn’t mean it is inherently bad or good for you,” he said. “The source of the food and the additives like preservatives, flavorings, sugars, and pigments that are added to increase palatability probably play a much larger role in increasing cancer risk.”

“A whole grain cereal and a hot dog are both UPF, but they push risk in opposite directions,” Thanki noted.

In their study, the National Cancer Institute researchers analyzed data from 461,682 adults aged 50 to 71 years who enrolled in the NIH-AARP Diet and Health Study between 1995 and 1996.

The participants recorded their eating habits using a food frequency questionnaire. Researchers then used that data to estimate each person’s intake of ultra-processed foods. The median consumption of ultra-processed foods among participants was 43% of daily median intake.

The participants were then followed until 2018, for a median of nearly 19 years. The scientists reported that 10,075 cases of colorectal adenocarcinoma were diagnosed during that period.

The researchers reported no association between overall intake of ultra-processed foods and the incidence of colorectal cancer.

However, they said their findings varied by food type. Higher intake of whole grains, fiber, dairy products, and calcium derived from UPF sources was associated with lower colorectal cancer incidence, while meat from UPF sources was associated with higher incidence.

Researchers also found that replacing 10% of gram weight from UPF intake with minimally processed foods was associated with a 2% lower incidence of CRC.

The researchers acknowledged limitations to their study.

They noted that the participants were primarily older, white Americans. In addition, UPF intake was only measured once at the beginning of the study period, so the findings cannot account for changes in eating habits or the increasing availability of ultra-processed foods.

Nonetheless, Ashkan Farhadi, MD, a gastroenterologist at MemorialCare Orange Coast Medical Center in California, who wasn’t involved in the study, said he found the results “very interesting.”

“The definition of ultra-processed foods is so broad,” he told Healthline. “It’s important to designate what type of ultra-processed foods you’re talking about.”

“You shouldn’t just go by whether a food is designated as ultra-processed,” Farhadi added. “You should go by what’s on the [ingredient] label.”

Shams-White shared a similar approach. “When it comes to diet, it is important to follow an overall healthy dietary pattern,” she told Healthline. “Emphasize a variety of fruits and vegetables and whole grains and limit red and processed meats, sugar-sweetened beverages, ultra-processed foods, and refined grain products.”

“Eating a diet rich in fiber and whole grains, dairy and calcium, and limiting processed and red meat and alcohol is what really reduces your risk of developing cancer,” added Thanki.

The American Cancer Society estimates there will be about 108,000 new cases of colon cancer and nearly 50,000 new cases of rectal cancer in the United States in 2026.

The incidence rate is slightly higher in men than in females.

The organization reports that the rate of colorectal cancer cases in the United States has declined since the mid-1980s, but they note that most of that decrease has occurred in older adults.

The incidence rate among people under 50 increased by nearly 3% from 2013 to 2022. Colorectal cancer is now the leading cause of death from cancer for U.S. adults under the age of 50.

Colorectal cancer occurs when cells in the large intestine grow out of control. About 70% of cases begin in the colon.

There are a number of symptoms of colorectal cancer. Some of the common ones include:

Diet is considered one of the risk factors for colorectal cancer. However, there are other considerations.

Farhadi said genetics, obesity, smoking, alcohol consumption, and a sedentary lifestyle can also increase a person’s risk of developing colorectal cancer.

Shams-White noted that the American Cancer Society Guideline for Diet and Physical Activity for Cancer Prevention recommended achieving and maintaining a healthy weight, being physically active, following a healthy eating pattern, and avoiding alcohol and tobacco.

Thanki points out that there are risk factors for colorectal cancer that can be modified and others that can’t.

“Among non-modifiable factors, the biggest are age, a personal or family history of colorectal cancer or advanced polyps, inherited syndromes such as Lynch syndrome, and longstanding inflammatory bowel disease (ulcerative colitis or Crohn’s colitis),” he told Healthline.

“On the modifiable side, the evidence is strongest for obesity, physical inactivity, smoking, alcohol, and diets high in red and processed meat and low in fiber, whole grains, and calcium,” he added.

Colorectal cancer treatment outcomes improve if the disease is caught at an early stage. The 5-year relative survival for localized colorectal cancer is 91.3%. The 5-year relative survival rate for colorectal cancer caught at various stages, including cancer that has spread, is 65.4%.

Shams-White points out that the American Cancer Society Colorectal Cancer Guidelines recommend that people at average risk of colorectal cancer start getting screened at age 45.

“Screening can help prevent cancer by finding abnormal cells and polyps so they can be removed before they can become colorectal cancer, as well as detect cancer at an earlier stage,” she said.

Thanki had similar advice. “Get screened starting at 45, or earlier if you have a family history or other risk factors, because colonoscopies can prevent cancer by removing polyps,” he said. “And never ignore symptoms like rectal bleeding or a change in bowel habits at any age.”

#4797. Veterans Day, Service, Music, and Gratitude

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 8, 2026 | Reviewed by Jessica Schrader

“Thank you for your service.” At a checkout counter, at an airport, or in a hallway, there’s rarely time to say much more. We offer our thanks and continue with the day.

At a Veterans Day ceremony, music could give us a little longer to consider what we’re thanking someone for.

When a bugler plays “Taps,” people grow quiet. Some bow their heads; others look toward the flag or watch the musician. Someone remembering a friend’s funeral may find those notes difficult to hear. A child attending a ceremony for the first time may look to a parent to understand why everyone has stopped talking. We hear the same music, but it brings different memories to each of us.

The national anthem gathers us in another way. Some people sing confidently; others search for a comfortable octave or stand silently. For a few minutes, we give our attention to something we share. What we make of that moment varies, especially in a country where our disagreements run deep. Still, it can be moving to hear people make the effort to sing together. And we may respectfully wonder about those who don’t stand.

Ceremonies have their place. We come together to honor, to remember, and to share those who have served and what we have in common as Americans. We also want to know more about the people we have gathered to honor.

People leave military service with very different feelings about their time in uniform. Some speak readily about it. Others have little interest in revisiting those years, particularly with someone they barely know. Pride may sit alongside grief or disappointment. Friendships can endure for a lifetime, as can questions about what happened and why.

A song may open a conversation. Maybe it was the one everyone complained about in the barracks, then sang along anyway. Someone else might remember listening through headphones during a long wait, or hearing a recording sent from home. A ridiculous song might bring back a friend more vividly than a formal tribute. A love song might bring back the person waiting at home.

Playing a medley of the armed forces songs is interesting, inspiring, and even surprising. When we listened to the medley, we were surprised to know the words or at least remember the tune to every song. They stir deeply, each bringing back a memory, an image. They do remind us to honor the service of individuals and the corps of fellow citizens who helped ensure and sustain our democracy.

We know how a few bars of music can take us somewhere: to the kitchen of a childhood home, a college roommate, a drive we had almost forgotten. For a veteran, a song from those years may be welcome, painful, or both.

“What did you listen to then?” gives someone room to decide where to begin and how much to share. The answer may have little to do with combat or sacrifice. It may be about being nineteen, missing home, or discovering a musician whose recordings became a lifelong companion.

We would like to hear more of those stories in the ways we observe Veterans Day. A school could invite a veteran to choose a piece of music and talk about its place in their life. A community concert could include songs local veterans suggest, along with the memories they choose to share. At home, a family might listen to a recording together and discover something they had never thought to ask.

We may hear an account that unsettles our assumptions about service. Someone may prefer to talk about the music itself. If they do, we can follow their lead.

Veterans Day also gives the rest of us reason to examine our responsibilities. Freedom, equality, the rule of law, and human dignity depend on what people do in ordinary civic life. Honoring service includes caring for veterans and their families, and considering how faithfully we uphold the ideals we invoke at ceremonies.

This Veterans Day reminds us that we are seeking a more perfect union and that we are one people. With gratitude.

This November, I hope we make time for the familiar tributes and for a few personal songs. After the ceremony, someone beside us may have a story about a recording they’ve kept for fifty years, or a friend who always sang off-key.

#4796. Toyota reveals five new lifted Woodland concepts, including the bZ electric SUV

Toyota introduced a new family of lifted, “adventure-ready” Woodland concepts based on the RAV4, Grand Highlander, Sienna, Crown Signia, and bZ electric SUV.

Toyota is the latest automaker to chase the highly profitable off-road market in the US, with plans to expand its “Woodland” lineup.

Although it already sells Woodland versions of the RAV4, Sienna, bZ, and most recently, the Grand Highlander, Toyota said the new family of concept vehicles is “designed for drivers who see adventure not as a destination, but a way of life.”

Toyota’s North American design studio, CALTY Design Research, designed the concepts to explore how some of its most popular nameplates can be used better on and off the road.

Each vehicle features Horizon Blue exterior paint, inspired by Toyota’s 1960s models, including the Stout, Crown, and Corona.

All new concepts also include an exclusive Woodland badge, plus a lift kit, large over-fenders, satin-black wheels, All-Terrain tires, two-tone paint on the roof and hood, a roof rack, and cross bars to top it off.

According to Toyota, the RAV4 Woodland Plug-In Hybrid and Sienna Woodland Concepts show how its “electrified and family-focused vehicles take on a more adventurous role.”

The electric Woodland bZ Concept “extends the Woodland theme into Toyota’s battery electric future.” Meanwhile, the Grand Highlander Woodland Concept and Crown Signia Woodland Concept bring two distinct models to the lineup, Toyota said.

The company didn’t reveal any powertrain specs or other details, but said the concepts show how capability can take many forms, including PHEV, hybrid, and battery electric.

Toyota’s new Woodland Concepts will be on display at the 2026 SEMA Show, starting on November 3.

To give you an idea, the 2027 Toyota bZ Woodland comes standard with a dual-motor all-wheel-drive (AWD) powertrain, delivering a combined 375 horsepower. That’s an extra 37 hp compared to the standard bZ with AWD.

The bZ Woodland also adds off-road capabilities with 8.3″ of ground clearance and the ability to tow up to 3,500 lbs.

Other rugged upgrades include All-Terrain tires, black side molding, roof rails, and black wheel arch cladding.

The 2027 Toyota bZ Woodland is available in Base and Premium trims, starting at $45,380, or over $10,000 more than the standard bZ.

#4795. Letter from the Editor-in-Chief: What Breast Cancer Patients Need When Treatment Ends

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Supporting your health & well-being at every stage of your breast cancer journey

Resources to support your emotional health and well-being

Tips for nourishing your body and mind while living with breast cancer

Navigating your next steps after diagnosis

A guide to medications, treatments, and procedures for breast cancer

Guide to symptoms, tests, and screenings for early detection

Resources to support you during remission or recurrence

Breast cancer awareness has never been higher. Every October, the world turns pink and the key messages—that early diagnosis saves lives and that knowing the risk factors reduces the risk—are hard to miss.

Breast cancer remains the leading cause of cancer death amongst women in most countries, with an estimated 694,000 deaths annually and around 8.2 million women globally living with a breast cancer diagnosis, according to 2024 data from the World Health Organization (WHO)’s Global Health Observatory.

But when October ends, and the wall-to-wall campaigns move on, what has awareness actually changed for those impacted by breast cancer?

For Marisa Weiss, MD, the answer is that there is always more to be done, and she’s uniquely placed to hold that view.

Dr. Weiss has treated breast cancer patients for more than 30 years. In 2000, she founded Breastcancer.org, a not-for-profit that provides expert-reviewed medical and lifestyle information on breast health and breast cancer to millions of people globally.

Sixteen years ago, she was diagnosed with stage 1 breast cancer, becoming, in her own words, a “dual citizen” in that moment, with lived experience on both sides of the doctor’s desk.

I had the pleasure of sitting down with Dr. Weiss as part of Healthline’s Breast Cancer Awareness Month coverage to talk about how awareness has changed care for the better for millions of people around the world, but why critical gaps remain, and how access to trusted information and community can help close those gaps.

“It’s good that awareness is high, but knowledge remains low,” she said. The misconception she sees most is the belief that breast cancer is something that happens to other families.

“Most people think they’re off the hook because it doesn’t run in their family,” Dr. Weiss explained. In fact, 85%-90% of people who get breast cancer have no known family history and no known gene in the family, “so we’re all at risk,” she warns.

For most, a diagnosis arrives as a shock. “They’re completely surprised, flattened by it. Their life is upside down, and they scramble to find what they need to know,” Dr. Weiss noted.

That aftershock caused by a diagnosis is at the core of why Breastcancer.org exists. Because the person whose life is at stake is increasingly expected to direct their own care and advocate for their needs, access to accurate and empowering information is critical in that process. “Decisions aren’t being made around the patient and for the patient in a bubble,” Dr. Weiss said. “Decision-making is supposed to be shared.”

With appointments hard to get and clinicians stretched, she said patients have to do more of the work.

In practice, Dr. Weiss says that means preparing by writing down your family history on both sides and making sure your care team knows who you are. “What’s important to you? Who’s in your life? Do you want more children? Are you planning a vacation? All those decisions can have an impact on the care you receive.”

Where Dr. Weiss sees the widest gap is after treatment ends. Speaking from personal experience, she said: “I had the best care possible, and there were still gaps. You can find yourself alone with lots of questions and fears.”

Understandably, a great deal of focus and attention is centered on diagnosis and treatment, she said. Then it stops. “When your life is supposed to go back to normal, it never does. You have to find a new normal. That quiet phase can be really lonely and difficult.”

For Dr. Weiss, the questions that fill that silence are often as practical as they are emotional: “How do I know my treatment is working? How do I tell leftover side effects from new ones? How do I go back to work, and who do I tell? How do I talk to my kids? What about that new treatment I heard about on TV last night?”

That post-treatment period can also be the first time anyone has really had a chance to stop, take stock, and start asking “what next?”

“You might think, what happened to me? Who do I want to be moving forward? How do I have a long life full of wonderful things, and remain as independent as possible?”

Some of what patients do post-care never reaches their doctor at all, with Dr. Weiss pointing to a growing amount of personal care happening outside the hospital: GLP-1s, peptides, hormonal therapies, supplements, medical cannabis, to name a few. Breastcancer.org’s annual Pulse survey shows that people reported being interested in all of those things and more, and that they tend to learn about them online rather than risk the stigma of bringing them up with their doctors.

“They don’t really trust that their doctor knows much about these things,” she said, “and they don’t want a conversation that makes them feel judged. Some patients worry about what ends up in their medical record and then everyone’s going to know.”

Dr. Weiss says the stakes are real, because some of those choices can interact with cancer medications with potential for adverse or unexpected side effects. “That is why people turn to Breastcancer.org with questions that are personal, private, and important, including “what do I need to share with my doctor, and who’s on a need-to-know basis?”

Peer communities fill part of that gap. “Breastcancer.org’s members share medical information, tips, and practical advice with people who have just had the call, or are about to start treatment and don’t know what to expect,” Dr. Weiss shared, and said that while she values that kind of support system hugely, it does come with a caveat:

The same community can also be intrusive. Dr. Weiss describes standing at a party, drink in hand, when someone asks what kind of cancer you had, what you did, and whether it came back. Her advice to patients, which she took herself: “Put up your hand and say, ‘thank you so much for caring, but I cannot hear another story right now.’”

On the topic of AI and its impact on treatment and care, Dr. Weiss is cautiously optimistic. On the treatment front, she points to tools that help radiologists read mammograms more thoroughly and assess future risk as game changers in the fight against breast cancer.

Breastcancer.org also uses AI for tasks such as finding citations and interpreting pathology reports. But like many, she is wary of misinformation. “When you’re fearful, you look for reassurance, and you don’t want to be reassured by misinformation. When it comes to health information, every word matters.”

Her final advice is for the appointment itself, which she says she has even struggled with. “When they start speaking quickly in complex medical language, you can get lost really fast. The risk is you kind of fake it. That must not happen.”

“Do your research in advance. Write things down. Bring someone you trust as a second set of ears. Ask direct questions. Don’t worry if it sounds funny or silly. It’s always a smart question when you are dealing with your health.” Just be prepared for the questions to multiply from there. “Once you get a certain set of questions answered, that raises more questions. So just write it all down.”

If breast cancer has touched your life, know that you are not alone. Healthline’s Bezzy Breast Cancer Community is a space for peer support, feel-good stories, and advice in a welcoming, stigma-free environment when your lived experience is seen, heard and valued.

Robin Hough is the Editor-in-Chief of Healthline, and in addition to this regular Letter from the Editor column, he can be found every other Saturday in our Healthline Daily newsletter. He’ll soon be launching a dedicated Letter from the Editor newsletter coming to an inbox near you later in the fall.

#4793. Coping With an Acute Injury or Health Diagnosis

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 8, 2026 | Reviewed by Jessica Schrader

Many clients who come to see me in therapy are coping with an acute injury or health change. For example, they may have sustained an injury while playing a sport or been given a new medical diagnosis. A sudden injury or health change can feel shocking and is often difficult to cope with. You may be trying to adjust to changes in mobility and functioning and worried about when and if you will return to your “normal” self.

Often, the most pressing concern is: Will I get better? And when? The uncertainty is difficult to tolerate. While some injuries or diagnoses have clear treatment plans and timelines, more often it is not crystal clear what someone’s recovery or medical journey will look like. The anxious brain likes to jump to worst-case scenarios when uncertainty exists. It takes a “better safe than sorry” approach, leading us to think about all the possible horrible outcomes so we can be prepared. However, these worst-case scenarios may never come to pass, and anxiety can start to take up more and more space in your daily life.

An injury or new diagnosis can feel like a never-ending emotional roller coaster ride that you never wanted to take. It can be challenging to acknowledge the reality of the injury or diagnosis, including sudden changes you may be facing, without thinking that your life is doomed. Below are some strategies for coping with an acute injury or health diagnosis.

It is helpful to be informed about your condition, as a general understanding can help you have effective conversations with health care providers. It is useful to use reputable sources for gathering information, and your medical team may be able to offer resources. Keep in mind that not all of your questions may have firm answers, and there may be limits to what you or your medical team may be able to know.

While it is difficult to tolerate uncertainty, be mindful of not going down an information-gathering rabbit hole that consumes too much of your time and life. If you notice that trying to gather information about your condition is taking over your daily life or that your anxiety is increasing, set time limits for gathering information. For example, 30 to 60 minutes a week.

A sudden injury or diagnosis can create a wave of emotions. You may feel scared, apprehensive, sad, angry, frustrated, etc. Trying to suppress your emotions can intensify them. Find an authentic way to express how you are feeling. For example, take five to 10 minutes daily to write out your thoughts or feelings, say them aloud on a voice memo app, or share how you are feeling with a trusted friend or family member. If it feels unfamiliar and anxiety-provoking to talk about your feelings, consider doing so in a less focused or pressured environment. For instance, you may talk about your feelings while traveling in the car with soft music playing.

It can be unfamiliar and challenging for some people to accept help from others. Maybe you are used to doing everything yourself, and accepting help leads you to feel incapable. However, accepting help from others allows people who care about you to be of assistance during a difficult time. This is beneficial for them as well as for you. Also, spend time with people you are comfortable with and enjoy. It is natural to feel down, withdraw from others, and isolate ourselves during stressful periods. Yet, isolation can worsen mood. Even if you don’t initially feel like it, carve out some time with others. Your desire to be with others may increase over time. Also, it may be helpful to seek out connection with others who have the same injury or diagnosis. Talking with others with a shared understanding and hearing about others’ treatments, recovery, and coping strategies can feel relieving and supportive.

It can be difficult to accept limitations or the reality that there are some things you may not be able to do or need to do in a different way. It is important to give yourself space and time to grieve any losses you are experiencing. Expecting too much of yourself or trying to ignore the current circumstances can lead to increased frustration, anger, and sadness. Also, trying to meet unrealistic goals may deplete you and lead to less functioning and ability than you would have if you set more realistic and sustainable goals.

Just because you have limitations or there are certain things you cannot do does not mean you are incapable. Non-judgmentally ask yourself what you can and want to realistically take on, and aim to set small, doable goals.

A new injury or diagnosis can be anxiety-provoking and scary, and can highlight what or who you care most about. Certain activities may be different now, yet there are likely things or people who continue to be meaningful to you. Carve out time for them. Stay connected, or reconnect, to what feels most important and fulfilling to you. You may find that many of these things are simple and joyful, such as spending time with loved ones or time in nature.

The anxious part of our minds equates uncertainty with bad based on self-protection and preservation. While a good outcome is not guaranteed, neither is a bad one. The future could be incredibly difficult, and it also could be better than you are thinking or neutral. When your mind wants to leap ahead to worst-case scenarios, pause, take a slow breath, and remind yourself, “Uncertain does not mean bad; it simply means unknown.” Then refocus on the present moment and a values-based action you can take today.

#4792. Tesla drops car referral rewards, now pays owners in FSD for referrals

Tesla has launched a new referral program in the US that pays owners in Full Self-Driving (Supervised) instead of rewarding car sales. A referred owner gets one free month of FSD, and the referrer gets a free month or a $99 Tesla Credit if that person starts paying.

At the same time, Tesla’s Refer and Earn terms no longer list any vehicle as a qualifying purchase for buyer or referrer rewards. Buy a Tesla with a friend’s code today and neither of you gets anything.

To share a link, you need to be paying for FSD (Supervised) monthly or own it outright from before Tesla stopped selling it, according to Tesla’s FSD referral support page. Owners who got FSD through a one-year grant can’t participate. The link lives under “Refer and Earn” in the Tesla app, version 4.62.0 or later.

The person on the other end has to own a registered Tesla with compatible hardware, can’t have paid for FSD in the past 12 months, and can’t have bought it outright. There’s also a catch for recent buyers: anyone who got a free FSD trial with a new car is locked out of referral links until 12 months after that trial ends.

The bigger change is buried in Tesla’s Refer and Earn page. Buyer benefits now apply to solar panels only. Referrer benefits cover solar, first demo drives (up to 30 over an account’s lifetime) and the new FSD referral.

Model 3, Model Y and Cybertruck only show up under loyalty benefits, for existing owners buying another Tesla product. Model S and Model X aren’t listed at all.

Tesla didn’t announce the change. The page is stamped “Updated February 24, 2026,” so it’s unclear exactly when vehicles came off the list.

That’s quite a turn for a program that was always about moving cars. When Tesla brought the referral program back in August 2024, a buyer got $1,000 off a Model S, X, Y or 3, and the referrer got $500 in credit. Tesla has killed and revived the program several times over the past decade, but cars were always at the center of it. Not anymore.

That’s the exact metric in Elon Musk’s 2025 CEO Performance Award, which includes a milestone of 10 million active FSD subscriptions. It’s the reason Tesla started disclosing the number in January in the first place.

The free month a friend receives doesn’t count toward that total. A paid conversion does, and that’s precisely the event the new program pays for.

The only way I would ever pay for FSD is if Tesla covered full comprehensive insurance for my vehicle and accepted all liability. Otherwise, it's a gamble with my (and others') life.

That they seem to prioritize this sham service (Just call it Assisted Driving for honesty sake?) versus improving the cars or lowering prices, tells me enough not to look at Tesla for my next vehicle.

The recipient has to already own a Tesla, so the program doesn’t add a single car to the fleet. It’s built to mine the existing fleet for subscriptions. Tesla had sold about 8.9 million vehicles by the end of 2025, and only 1.74 million are paying for FSD, so there’s plenty of room. At Q3’s pace, we estimated 10 million subscriptions is still about eight years away.

So Tesla stopped paying for referrals that require selling a car, and started paying for the ones that move the number in Musk’s pay package. We think that tells you a lot about where the company’s priorities are right now.

#4791. The Bestselling Protein Powder on Amazon Is Also Our Budget-Friendly Pick

We’ve been using Optimum Nutrition Gold Standard 100% Whey for years. Here’s what you need to know.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

THERE’S NEVER BEEN a better time to focus on your protein intake, with an arsenal of products ready to help you meet your macros. When tossing back chicken breast or sirloin isn't an option, protein powder is a valuable tool, especially when it comes to building lean muscle and promoting recovery. Unfortunately, most protein powders aren't cheap.

It's fair to be wary of budget options, especially if you use protein powder regularly. But there's an inexpensive protein powder that's an Amazon bestseller that's worth considering. It's called Optimum Nutrition Gold Standard 100% Whey, and we keep coming back to it. While it's not the cheapest protein powder you can find, the brand does a solid job balancing out nutritional needs and quality at a price tag most people can afford.

No protein powder is perfect, including this one. But with nearly 81,000 five-star reviews to back it up, plus an Informed Choice certification, you have to wonder if there's something to Optimum Nutrition Gold Standard. Two Men's Health editors put this powder to the test over several months, and have largely positive things to say about it. Keep these in mind before adding this protein powder to your cart.

The low price is what brings most people to the table for Optimum Nutrition Gold Standard 100% Whey. While price per serving varies depending on the size you buy, you're looking at $1.06 to $1.54 per serving, with more savings the larger the container you purchase.

By comparison, our best overall protein powder, Transparent Labs Grass-Fed Whey Protein Isolate, is $2 per serving. Should price be the main reason you choose a protein powder? Definitely not. But if you're able to get what you're looking for in an inexpensive powder, why wouldn't you go with it?

"The value is something to give props to," says MH Fitness and Reviews Editor Charles Thorp, NASM. The brand is able to keep the cost down because this isn't a pure whey protein isolate, Thorp explains. Instead, it's a blend of whey protein isolate, whey protein concentrate, and hydrolyzed whey protein. Still, that delivers 24g of protein and 5.5g of BCAAs per serving.

Texture matters with protein powder, and some can lean toward a sandy or gritty feel. That usually means it won't blend as well in your shake or smoothie, which can make it tough to keep using a product. But Optimum Nutrition has a light texture that blends easily.

"It’s fluffy, not sandy, like some protein powders," says MH Deputy Editor Paul Kita. "That tells me it’s going to blend well and won’t sit heavy in my gut." Thorp also praises Optimum Nutrition's texture. "The powder itself is lighter than the majority of other protein powders, which is nice because it opens up your options for mixers," he says. #4790. Women With Autoimmune Diseases More Likely to Be Misdiagnosed Than Men

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

A new international study found that women with autoimmune diseases often experience longer delays in getting a correct diagnosis compared to men.

The research, published in eClinicalMedicine on October 12, also shows that females report higher rates of being misdiagnosed, especially with mental health or psychosomatic conditions.

These findings highlight challenges in diagnosing autoimmune diseases and suggest that sex differences affect patients’ experiences in healthcare.

This is significant given that autoimmune diseases, conditions in which the body’s immune system attacks its own healthy cells, are estimated to affect around 4.6% of the U.S. population. Additionally, despite the observed disparities in diagnoses, women are almost two times as likely as men to be diagnosed with an autoimmune disease.

Researchers conducted an online survey between December 7, 2024, and March 7, 2025, inviting adults ages 18 and older who had a confirmed autoimmune or rheumatic disease.

The survey was carefully designed and tested with input from patients, charities, and medical experts to ensure it captured important information about patients’ diagnostic journeys.

Participants were asked about the time it took from when they first noticed symptoms to when they received their autoimmune diagnosis.

They also reported how many healthcare visits they made before diagnosis and whether they felt their symptoms were ever misdiagnosed as mental health issues, psychosomatic problems (physical symptoms caused or worsened by psychological factors), or another physical disease.

The survey was widely shared on social media, patient support groups, and community organizations to reach a broad audience.

Special efforts were made to include underrepresented groups such as males, younger individuals, and people from minority ethnic backgrounds.

The survey was available in five languages, and participants could complete it with help from researchers if needed.

To analyze the data, the team used statistical methods, adjusting for factors like age, type of autoimmune disease, continent of residence, and financial situation.

These methods helped compare the experiences of males and females while accounting for differences in disease types and other factors

The study included 6,607 participants, with 91.2% identifying as female and most living in the United Kingdom. On average, women were younger than men in the study.

Autoimmune thyroid disease was the most common condition reported. Non-autoimmune conditions like anxiety were more commonly reported by women, while men reported higher rates of hypertension.

One of the main findings was that women reported longer delays before getting a diagnosis. Nearly 32% of females experienced delays of four years or more from symptom onset to diagnosis, compared to about 26% of males.

On the other hand, men were more likely to be diagnosed within a year of symptom onset (nearly 50% of males versus 40% of females).

Women also made more visits to healthcare providers before diagnosis, with 26.2% having 11 or more visits compared to 18.4% of men.

When it came to misdiagnoses, women were significantly more likely to report that their symptoms had been mistaken for mental health issues (43.3% of females vs. 32.7% of males) or psychosomatic causes (33.9% of females vs. 21.5% of males).

However, there was no significant difference between men and women in being misdiagnosed with another physical disease.

The type of autoimmune disease also influenced misdiagnosis rates. Diseases with clear physical symptoms or definitive lab tests, like type 1 diabetes or rheumatoid arthritis, had lower rates of mental health and psychosomatic misdiagnoses.

In contrast, conditions such as autoimmune encephalitis or undifferentiated connective tissue disease had higher rates of these misdiagnoses (over 50%).

After adjusting for disease type and other factors, women still had higher odds of reporting mental health or psychosomatic misdiagnoses compared to men.

Other factors affected misdiagnosis rates, too. People living in continents outside the United Kingdom, those with lower household income, and certain disease groups were more likely to report psychiatric or psychosomatic misdiagnoses. Age, however, was not linked to the risk of being misdiagnosed.

Muhammad Qasim, MD, a pulmonologist and medical writer with MySleepApneaTeam, told Healthline that autoimmune diseases are often difficult to diagnose. Qasim wasn’t involved in the study.

“Early symptoms can be vague, fluctuate over time, and affect several parts of the body,” he said. “Fatigue, pain, sleep problems, brain fog, and mood changes do not immediately point to one diagnosis.”

Qasim echoed the study’s findings, explaining that similar symptoms may be interpreted differently in women versus men, with complaints being attributed to anxiety, stress, or psychosomatic causes.

However, there are probably multiple factors contributing to this phenomenon, he said.

“Differences in disease presentation, gaps in research, fragmented care, and unconscious bias can all contribute,” said Qasim. “Once a psychiatric explanation enters the medical record, there is also a risk that later clinicians view new symptoms through that same lens.”

Regarding unconscious bias, the study’s authors noted that women have historically been treated by doctors as “less credible” and more “emotional” in reporting their symptoms, which can influence how doctors interpret them.

These disparities in diagnosis are important, however, because longer waits and erroneous diagnoses can delay proper treatment and increase women’s frustration, leading them to stop asking for help.

The researchers suggest that healthcare providers need to be aware of these concerns and consider autoimmune diseases carefully when patients, especially females, present with more complicated symptoms.

Adam Carewe, MD, a physician in Boulder, CO, and a clinical informaticist with General Medicine who wasn’t involved in the study, offered guidance to those experiencing symptoms on how to obtain a proper diagnosis.

Healthgrades is owned by RVO Health. By clicking on this link, we may receive a commission. Learn more.

“Patients can keep an accurate symptom timeline, bring in family history, ask what else could be explaining these symptoms, ask for a plan for next steps if initial testing/treatment, do not change anything, and lastly get a second opinion,” he advised.

Carewe emphasized the value of not giving up on finding answers. “The most important thing for anyone with persistent symptoms of any kind is to continue to work with your primary care clinician and continue to advocate for yourself,” he said.

#4788. Flex Your Emotional Intelligence at Work

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 8, 2026 | Reviewed by Jessica Schrader

Therapy lingo has become a “thing” on social media, and it is helpful when it illuminates important psychological concepts like “gaslighting” or “trauma bonding.” It can be especially useful in a professional setting when being perceived as emotionally intelligent is important. Possibly the best by-product, however, is that it can prevent you from getting dragged into drama, aggressively taking a side, or bashing anyone. Essentially, by identifying the psychological dynamic beneath the surface, you are providing empathy and wisdom in a constructive and professional manner. Before you try it, however, you may want to do your research to ensure that you are using the terms correctly. Six examples may help clarify how it sounds.

Your teammate asks you to lunch because he needs help dealing with a colleague. He explains, “I told him that I was drawing a line and that I would not finish the project for him this time... The next thing I know, he is talking to everyone about me behind my back. He, literally, turned my closest co-worker against me. Now, they are work 'besties,' and neither of them will talk to me."

Response: That hurts, and it is so disappointing. It sounds like triangulation, which is very manipulative. I may have a book that can help.

You highlight that when the co-worker does not get what he wants from a person, he can be passive aggressive, aligning other people with him and against them, which is called “triangulation.”

Your work friend stops by your office because she is angry and needs to vent. She laments, “I cannot stand being on projects with Dave. I know he has had a hard life, but why do I have to suffer because of it? Every time there is work to do, he complains that he doesn’t feel good, or that the boss is being mean to him, or that his car broke down, or that he just got scammed, or that he is being evicted…. He gets out of doing any work every time! It is infuriating."

Response: It sounds like he uses a victim stance. That is so frustrating. I read somewhere that it is important to calmly and respectfully hold people accountable—no matter what.

You empathize with your friend, but also highlight the possibility of a cognitive distortion (victim stance) that may need to be confronted.

Your friend from another department calls and says, “I am so panicked when I am in meetings with Maureen. I work my tail off and do a fantastic job, which is backed by my client’s feedback and my stats, but she calls me 'lazy' and 'apathetic' in front of everyone."

Response: That is so humiliating, and those sound like mischaracterizations. You are none of those things. She may be threatened by your competence and is struggling to handle her jealousy in a healthy manner.

By reassuring her that you believe she is being misperceived, you are supporting her while alerting her to the possibility that the colleague may not be managing her envy in a mature way. When her colleague name-calls, she may be “projecting.”

You ask your co-worker to grab lunch, but she says she can’t because of her suitemate. She says, “Chad needs a lot of help. I feel sorry for him. I help him with all of his projects, and I finish his quotes because he is not good with numbers, but he still throws a fit about his workload, so I end up working through lunch every day just to try and help."

Response: You feel for Chad, which makes you a good person in my opinion, but it sounds like it has become codependent. My therapist usually advises me to detach and get perspective with certain people. By taking a step back, I can figure out whether I am enabling the person.

This example uses multiple psychosocial terms: codependent, detachment, and enabling, to illuminate the problematic nature of the relationship, and the need for an intervention.

A colleague comes to your office and says, “I really like working with Lisa, but she is so clingy. She cannot do anything without me. I tried to go for walks on my breaks last week and she insisted on coming with me every time. I cannot even go to the bathroom without her following me."

Response: That’s frustrating. She may have an anxious attachment style. I know how aggravating it can be. Even though it’s difficult, I try to calmly and kindly set boundaries in those situations.

You are identifying the root of the problem is the person’s attachment style, which may not change, so the person may need to implement limits in the relationship.

A co-worker approaches you and confides, "Ann continually and incessantly criticizes me for things, but she turns around and does the exact same thing. I cannot take it. She is such a hypocrite."

Response: That is so irritating. It sounds like she may have deficits with insight and self-awareness.

In this example, you empathize, but also suggest that there may be a flaw in Ann's emotional maturity, that may prevent her from embodying emotionally intelligent tendencies.

Work relationships can be difficult and continually getting dragged into the middle of drama can be time-consuming and anxiety-inducing. However, the last thing you want is to come off as aloof, detached, and unsupportive of others. You strive to be a safe person to talk to. By attempting to identify the dysfunctional dynamic in a problematic situation, you avoid attacking and bad-mouthing colleagues, which helps you maintain a high level of professionalism. You can find even more information on this topic in my book, How to Outsmart a Narcissist, Use Emotional Intelligence to Regain Control at Home, at Work, and in Life.

#4787. BYD reveals a flashy new feature on its upcoming luxury EV

BYD is moving upmarket with its new flagship EV, featuring suicide doors, a gemstone grille, and possibly solid-state batteries.

Yangwang is like BMW’s Rolls-Royce and Mercedes-Maybach, sitting at the very top of BYD’s brand hierarchy.

The ultra-luxury brand offers BYD’s most high-end and technically advanced vehicles, including the U7 sedan, the U8, a hardcore off-road SUV, and the U9, an electric supercar.

Yangwang vehicles have previously debuted with BYD’s latest breakthrough tech, including its quad-motor e4 platform (delivering over 1,300 hp), its second-generation Blade Batteries and Flash Charging, and its DiSus-X intelligent body control system.

Its next model will push further into the elite segment. After BYD revealed the name of its new flagship executive sedan earlier this week, the Yangwang Altior, the company has released several new details ahead of its official debut.

Yangwang general manager Hu Xiaoqing confirmed on Friday that the new Yangwang Altior will feature suicide doors, a first for a BYD model.

The new door design swings open nearly 90 degrees, Hu said, creating a dramatic, wide-open entrance.

Hu also posted a preview of the vehicle’s front fascia, complete with a dot-matrix Gemstrone grille and crystal-inspired headlights.

BYD has not confirmed many details, but the ultra-luxury sedan is expected to be about 5,500 mm (216″) in length.

Images of the disguised vehicle released last month show a similar shape and size to the Mercedes-Benz Maybach S-Class or Rolls-Royce Phantom.

HU said last week that the global launch of the new flagship sedan will take place in the UAE, not in BYD’s home market of China.

BYD has not revealed an official date, but according to CarNewsChina, citing “sources familiar with the project,” BYD aims to unveil the new flagship model in Dubai, UAE, around November 5.

The Yangwang Altrio will feature “unprecedented disruptive technology,” Zheng Yu, Yangwang’s executive general manager, said.

In one image, the vehicle was charging at a BYD Flash Charge station, suggesting it will use its Blade Battery 2.0 and 5-minute Flash Charging technology.

There are companies showcasing flying cars designed specifically for circus-style shows, while others are launching solid-state batteries that can recharge in five minutes.

I find myself wondering—though perhaps not too deeply—which of these technologies will secure the largest customer base and generate the greatest returns for shareholders.

Outside of the suicide doors, rumors suggest the flagship model will be BYD’s first vehicle to use solid-state batteries. Executive vice president Stella Li said during an interview with Carwow.es last month that BYD’s first vehicle to use solid-state batteries will debut in 2027.

The executive sedan is expected to debut around November 5. Prices are rumored to start in the 2 million yuan range, or about $300,000.

Yangwang’s current electric sedan, the U7, starts at 658,000 yuan ($98,000). The extended U8L, on the other hand, is the brand’s highest-priced mass-produced vehicle, starting at 1.45 million yuan ($217,000).

#4786. Honda has dominated motorcycles for decades. Electric bikes are changing that

Honda has spent decades building one of the most dominant positions in the global motorcycle industry, selling millions of gasoline-powered two-wheelers each year. But in markets where electric motorcycles and scooters are becoming increasingly accessible, that dominance is starting to face a serious challenge.

Vietnam offers a particularly interesting case study, where rapidly growing electric motorcycle sales are beginning to reshape a market long dominated by Honda.

According to newly released nationwide sales figures, Vietnam saw more than 3 million motorcycle and scooter sales during the first nine months of 2026, representing 25.9% growth over the same period last year.

But the real story is in the electric segment, where sales surged 90.5% to reach 973,247 units. That means electric two-wheelers now account for approximately 32% of all new motorcycle and scooter sales in the country.

And the biggest beneficiary isn’t Honda. It’s actually Vietnamese electric vehicle manufacturer VinFast.

While Honda remains Vietnam’s largest motorcycle manufacturer overall, with sales growing 8.4% this year, VinFast has surged into second place with a staggering 152.1% increase in sales. Yamaha now sits in third place, followed by electric two-wheeler manufacturer Yadea in fourth.

Of the top four players, half are electric, and it’s precisely that half that is experiencing meteoric sales growth.

It’s an impressive reshuffling of a market that has traditionally been dominated by Japanese gasoline motorcycle manufacturers.

Vietnam’s transition hasn’t happened in a vacuum, either. Government efforts to reduce urban air pollution, including plans to restrict gasoline-powered motorcycles in parts of Hanoi, have helped create an increasingly favorable environment for electric alternatives.

Too bad for Honda but I'm thrilled to read about increasing sales of electric motorcycles. I don't live in or near Vietnam but the pollution from small gasoline engines affects everyone where the wind blows it.

And with companies like VinFast offering an expanding range of electric scooters and motorcycles, riders now have more practical alternatives to gasoline-powered models than ever before.

To be clear, Honda isn’t exactly struggling. Its motorcycle sales are still growing, and the Japanese giant remains the undisputed market leader in Vietnam. But its overall share of the market is shrinking, and its relatively modest growth compared to the exploding electric segment suggests that the market’s center of gravity is beginning to shift.

Vietnam may be just a single example, but it’s an important one of what can happen when electric two-wheelers become viable mainstream alternatives to gasoline motorcycles.

Honda has spent decades perfecting the gasoline motorcycle. The question now is how quickly it can adapt to a market that is increasingly interested in something else.
